title: Evaluating the Accuracy and Quality of Breastfeeding-Related Information on Instagram
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 80 top-performing Instagram posts drawn from four breastfeeding hashtags (April 25-30, 2025). Every post was scored 1-4 for accuracy against CDC, WHO and AAP guidelines with explicit inaccurate categories, giving a share of items that were inaccurate (36.3% mostly or completely inaccurate; 16.3% completely inaccurate) — guideline concordance stated as accurate/inaccurate, hence CONTENT. The Global Quality Scale results are recorded separately as a QUALITY row.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language posts; authors based in the United States)
estimates.date: Posts manually collected between April 25 and April 30, 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of top-performing breastfeeding Instagram posts scored mostly or completely inaccurate against CDC/WHO/AAP guidelines
estimates.value_raw: 36.3% were either mostly or completely inaccurate (Table 2: score of 1 = 13 (16.3%), score of 2 = 16 (20%), of N = 80)
estimates.denominator: 80 eligible "top posts" (20 from each of #breastfeeding, #breastfeedingeducation, #breastfeedinghacks, #pumpingmama) containing explicit English-language breastfeeding advice; over 430 posts were screened to reach this 80
estimates.definition: Post assigned an accuracy score of 1 ("completely inaccurate") or 2 ("mostly inaccurate but a small proportion of statements are accurate") when its breastfeeding claims were compared against established CDC, WHO and AAP guidelines
estimates.misinfo_def: "Posts were assigned a minimum score of one if they were completely inaccurate, and a maximum score of four if they were completely accurate and fully aligned with official guidelines."
estimates.source_quote: Overall, 38.8% of posts were completely accurate, while 36.3% were either mostly or completely inaccurate.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two raters scored each post sequentially on a 4-point accuracy framework adapted from Dennis et al., benchmarked against CDC, WHO and AAP breastfeeding guidelines; a third independent rater decided any disagreement. No kappa or other agreement statistic is reported, and the authors list 'multiple raters' as needed future work.
estimates.moderator_quote: For each hashtag, only 20 "top posts," as displayed by Instagram's search algorithm, were screened to focus on the most visible and influential content. The "top" section of Instagram search results prioritizes posts with high visibility and engagement metrics such as views, likes, and shares.
estimates.notes: CONTENT, not QUALITY: posts were judged against an external ground truth (official CDC/WHO/AAP guidance) on a scale whose low anchors are explicitly 'inaccurate', so a wholly accurate post cannot score 1 or 2. The 36.3% is stated verbatim in the abstract and Results, so it is not a cross-category sum computed by me; it is corroborated by Table 2 (13 + 16 = 29 of 80 = 36.25%). denom_selection = curated: engagement-ranked 'top posts' only, 20 per hashtag, with ineligible posts replaced by the next eligible one. confidence = medium because the sample is small, engagement-truncated, and no interrater reliability statistic is given.

estimates.notes: QUALITY construct per the governing rule (GQS measures clarity/usefulness/presentation, not truth), so this row must be excluded from prevalence pooling. Only the GQS = 1 share is used: the 1.3% scoring 2 is a separate verbatim cell, and combining 3.8% + 1.3% into a 'poor quality' share would be a forbidden cross-category sum. source_quote is the Table 2 block (mean GQS and the count scoring 1) because the prose sentence is column-interleaved in the extracted text; the prose reads: 'The mean general quality score was 4.0 (SD = 1.03), with the majority of posts rated as good or excellent quality. Nonetheless, 3.8% of the posts were rated as very poor quality and 1.3% as generally poor.'

missed_or_uncertain: 1) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES an adjudicator should see. (a) The reported mean accuracy of 3.7 (SD 1.41) is arithmetically impossible given the paper's own distribution (13x1 + 16x2 + 20x3 + 31x4 = 229/80 = 2.86). The shares I extracted come from the distribution and the abstract, which agree with each other (31/80 = 38.75% completely accurate, 29/80 = 36.25% mostly/completely inaccurate), so the error appears to be in the mean, not the shares. (b) The Discussion states 'our findings showed that 40% of posts were mostly accurate', but Table 2 gives 20/80 = 25% at score 3; the 40% figure matches instead the share scoring GQS = 5 ('40% of the Instagram posts in our study achieved the maximum Global Quality Score (GQS) of 5', 32/80), so the Discussion sentence looks like a transposition. (c) Table 2 labels every accuracy and GQS row 'Videos with a total score of...' although the counts sum to all 80 posts, 45 of which are pictures — a labelling error, not a sample restriction. (d) Table 2 lists the health-care-worker share as 35 (43.8%) while the text says 'Nearly half (44%)' and later '44% of top posts'; immaterial to the extracted rows. 2) Not extracted: the 38.8% completely accurate and 25% mostly accurate shares (accuracy, not misinformation, and complements of the extracted rows); the 1.3% scoring GQS = 2; all ordered-logistic ORs by format, account type and topic (associations, not prevalences); the 5.23 OR for health-professional quality. 3) Account-type and format subgroup accuracy shares are not reported as percentages, only as ORs, so no subgroup rows are possible. 4) '430 videos screened to include 80 posts' is an eligibility funnel, not a misinformation share. 5) Figures quoted from other studies (44% accurate / 46.5% misleading on Facebook; 19% good-or-excellent on YouTube) are cited from elsewhere and excluded under R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional observational content analysis. Purposive, engagement-truncated sample: four breastfeeding hashtags (#breastfeeding, #breastfeedingeducation, #breastfeedinghacks, #pumpingmama), 20 Instagram 'top posts' each, collected 25-30 April 2025 from a newly created account to avoid personalisation; over 430 posts screened, ineligible ones replaced by the next eligible post until 80 were reached. Eligibility: English, explicit breastfeeding advice, publicly available; excluded personal stories, promotional-only, duplicates, pump-mechanics-only. Accuracy scored 1-4 against CDC/WHO/AAP guidelines (framework adapted from Dennis et al.); quality scored on the 5-point Global Quality Scale. Two raters sequentially, third rater resolving disagreements; NO interrater reliability statistic reported. Analysis in STATA 17, ordered logistic regression, alpha 0.05. IRB approval not required (public data). Authors' stated limits: top-posts-only sampling favours engagement over reliability, small sample, need for multiple raters.
rob.item6_quote: Posts were assigned a minimum score of one if they were completely inaccurate, and a maximum score of four if they were completely accurate and fully aligned with official guidelines. Posts that included content on other health topics beside breastfeeding, such as sleep, maternal wellbeing, or product promotion, were evaluated solely on their breastfeeding-related claims.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, 38.8% of posts were completely accurate, while 36.3% were either mostly or completely inaccurate.
